name: model-view-intent
intent: Structure one UI feature as a single loop in which every user interaction becomes an intent value, a pure reduce step derives the next immutable state from the previous state and that intent, and the view renders only that state - so the screen's behaviour is determined by data instead of by scattered event handlers.
problem: Presentation state is spread across the view, its presenter and several observable channels: every handler sets its own field or widget directly, a loading flag, a data field and an error field can contradict each other, the view keeps state of its own that a configuration change or process death destroys, and no state transition can be exercised without instantiating the UI.
context: Interactive applications with a declarative view layer and some reactive runtime - Android/Compose with coroutines and Flow, SwiftUI, React, Scala.js, or a hand-rolled event loop - where one screen or app-level feature can own a single immutable state object, user events can be represented as data values, and the view can re-render from a new state value. It is applied per feature, not per widget, and it is independent of any particular framework.
benefits: One source of truth per feature: every visible property comes from the one state object, so loading, empty, error and content variants cannot contradict each other.
Intents as data make interaction testable: reduce(state, intent) is a pure function, so transitions are asserted by comparing state values instead of verifying view calls or mounting widgets.
Reproducibility and debuggability: the current state plus the last intent describe the screen completely, which is enough to reproduce a crash, log a transition history or replay a session.
Lifecycle resilience: re-rendering the last state restores the screen after a configuration change or process recreation, because the view holds no hidden state of its own.
A single funnel for interaction: validation, logging, analytics and effect orchestration live in one intent handler instead of being repeated in every event listener.
Effects have an explicit home: one-shot work (navigation, toasts, network calls) runs outside the reducer and feeds results back as new intents, keeping the pure core free of I/O.
tradeoffs: Ceremony per screen: intent types, an immutable state type, a reducer, a state holder and an effects channel replace a mutable view model's fields, so small screens carry noticeably more code.

Every transition produces a new state value (or persistent-structure copies), and the state stream typically conflates equal values: at high interaction rates the allocation and copying cost is real, and huge state trees need splitting into sub-reducers.

The discipline is unenforced in most languages: mutating a published snapshot, handing out the mutable backing field, or letting the view keep a parallel copy breaks change detection and history while the app still appears to work.

One-shot events do not fit a state stream: keeping navigation or toast data in the state replays it whenever the state is re-emitted, re-rendered or restored - the 'SingleLiveEvent problem' - so an effects channel with different delivery semantics is mandatory.
Errors modelled as states grow the state union, and the view must handle every variant exhaustively; a missing or unhandled variant renders as stale or blank content rather than failing loudly.

Asynchronous intents need explicit ordering and cancellation: without a policy for stale results (latest-intent-wins, cancellation, ordering) a slow response from an earlier intent can overwrite a newer state.

participants.responsibility: A data value describing what the user wants to do (Refresh, Submit(text), Select(id)) - the only input the model accepts; intents name user intentions, not widget events.

Pure function (State, Intent) -> State that decides the next state, is the only code allowed to create it, returns the previous state for intents it does not handle, and delegates data work to business logic without performing I/O itself.
Immutable value object describing everything the screen displays, typically as explicit variants (loading, empty, error, content) rather than nullable flags.
Renders exactly one state through a single render(state) entry point and converts raw UI events into intent values; it makes no decisions and keeps no presentation state of its own.

Owns the current state, serializes intent handling, exposes the state as an observable stream (Flow/StateFlow, Observable, Combine, store) and drives re-rendering; retains state across view recreation.
Runs one-shot work outside the pure reducer - network calls, persistence, navigation, toasts, analytics - and delivers its results back into the loop as further intents or effects.

use_cases: A search or feed screen where loading, empty, error and result states are concurrent flags in the old design and must become one state value the view can render without contradictions.
Complex screen flows - checkout, wizards, media players, editors - whose transitions must be explicit and reviewable rather than emerging from scattered handler code.
Screens that must survive configuration changes or process death by restoring one serializable state object instead of replaying a history of view commands.
Crash reports and support cases that carry the current state plus the last intent, making reproduction and replay possible without reproducing the exact tap sequence.
Cross-platform features that share the reducer between platforms and swap only the view layer (Android and iOS, web and desktop).
Large applications where each feature module exposes an intent/state contract and different teams own the loop for their screens.
A Cycle.js component whose DOM and HTTP driver streams become intents, whose model derives state, and whose view renders that state is a direct stream-based MVI implementation.
A Kotlin Multiplatform feature built with Orbit MVI can share an OrbitContainer's intent, reduce, state, and side-effect flow across Android, iOS, and desktop.

An Android Jetpack Compose feature following Android's official unidirectional-data-flow guidance can use a ViewModel-owned immutable UiState, upward events, and downward rendering as a framework-native MVI realization.
avoid_when: The state is local to one widget and short-lived (a toggle, a hover flag, one form field): a framework-local slot (remember/useState/plain field) is simpler and has no shared readers.
A small screen whose mutable view model is well understood: MVVM or a presenter with one output per event costs less ceremony than intents, reducers and effects channels.

The framework already supplies a state holder with unidirectional flow (Android ViewModel + StateFlow, SwiftUI Observation, React useState) and the screen has few states: use that state holder directly - this is the lighter realization, not the full pattern.
High-frequency data (pointer tracking, audio levels, animation frames) that would be routed through intents and state emissions: keep it in the render/effect path and read it imperatively.
The domain is better described by a formal state machine with guarded transitions and a fixed lifecycle: a statechart/state pattern is clearer than an open-ended intent set.
The screen is a pure function of server state that a query cache (React Query/SWR/GraphQL client) already tracks; adding a reducer loop duplicates the cache.
anti_patterns: Intent as setter: intents that mirror widgets (SetLoadingTrue, SetErrorText) instead of naming a user intention (Refresh, SubmitOrder), pushing UI mechanics into the model.
A second source of truth: the view (or a leftover presenter) keeps its own copy of a field or flag while also rendering the state, so the two drift apart.
One-shot events stored in the state (a navigateTo field, an error message that never clears) so re-rendering or restoring the screen replays navigation and toasts.
Mutating state inside reduce, or publishing mutable collections, so previously emitted snapshots change retroactively and equality-based emission drops the update.
Reducers that call the network, the database or the clock: transitions stop being pure, tests need mocks, and replay stops reproducing the session.
Using a global intent/event bus as the loop: unordered delivery, no state ownership and no way to say which intent changed what.
design_principles: Single source of truth: one state object per feature, changed only by the reducer.
Unidirectional flow: intent -> reduce -> new state -> render, with no second path back into the state.
Pure core, imperative shell: reduce is a pure function; I/O, timers and navigation live at the boundary as effects.
Command-query separation with explicit intent: the view reports what the user wanted as data and reads rendered state; the model decides the consequences.
Immutability as the change protocol: each transition publishes a new value, which makes comparison, history and replay possible.
Exhaustive state modelling: state variants cover exactly the situations the screen can be in, and the view handles all of them.
best_practices: Name intents after user intentions or domain events (SubmitOrder, Refresh, Retry) rather than after widget events (ButtonClicked).
Keep the state minimal and serializable, and derive display-only data in the view or in selectors instead of storing it.
Implement one reducer function per feature as the only mutation path; compose sub-reducers when the state grows, and keep each one pure.
Model loading, empty, error and content as explicit state variants (sealed class, discriminated union, record hierarchy) instead of nullable flags.
Route one-shot effects (navigation, snackbars, analytics) through a dedicated effects channel, never through the state.
Expose the state as an immutable stream and let the view collect it lifecycle-aware; never hand out the mutable backing field.
Serialize intent handling (single dispatcher, main-thread confinement or an actor) so concurrent intents cannot interleave transitions.
Test reduce as a table-driven pure function and effects with a fake intent sink; keep the view layer thin enough that no widget tests are needed for transitions.
sources: Catalog provenance: Model-View-Intent as specified by Andre Medeiros (Staltz) for Cycle.js and brought to Android by Hannes Dorfmann's 'Reactive Apps with Model-View-Intent' series (2017, parts 1-8); catalog row 'Model-View-Intent', docs/design-patterns.md section 9 (Presentation state and coordination).
